claim: Mass spectrometry analysis identified Ser297 as being phosphorylated constitutively in hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP expressed in Flp-In T-REx 293 cells.
source: LC-MS/MS identified Ser297 as being phosphorylated constitutively, and Ser296/297 as being phosphorylated by sorbic acid or MOMBA.
evidence: Mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1 directly identifies phosphorylation at Ser297 in vehicle-treated samples.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis identified Ser296/297 as being phosphorylated by sorbic acid or MOMBA in hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP expressed in Flp-In T-REx 293 cells.
source: LC-MS/MS identified Ser297 as being phosphorylated constitutively, and Ser296/297 as being phosphorylated by sorbic acid or MOMBA.
evidence: Mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1 identifies phosphorylation at both Ser296 and Ser297 after agonist treatment.

claim: The pSer296/pSer297 antiserum can identify hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP in vehicle-treated cells.
source: The potential pSer296/pSer297 antiserum was able to identify a diffuse set of polypeptides centred at 70 kDa in preparations generated from vehicle-treated cells (Figure 2B)
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 2B shows detection of the receptor in vehicle-treated samples.

claim: The intensity of pSer296/pSer297 antiserum staining was increased in samples derived from cells after exposure to MOMBA.
source: the intensity of staining was increased in samples derived from cells after exposure to the hFFAR2-DREADD agonist MOMBA (Figure 2B).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 2B shows increased signal intensity after MOMBA treatment compared to vehicle.

claim: The pSer296/pSer297 antiserum was unable to identify hFFAR2-DREADD-PD1 (Ser296Ala/Ser297Ala variant) either with or without MOMBA exposure.
source: when samples were produced from a Flp-In T-REx 293 cell line induced to express a variant of hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP in which both Ser296 and Ser297 were converted to Ala (hFFAR2-DREADD-PD1) (Figure 2A and B) the potential pSer296/pSer297 antiserum was unable to identify the receptor protein either with or without exposure of the cells to MOMBA (Figure 2B).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 2B shows absence of signal for PD1 variant, confirming specificity of the antiserum for phosphorylated Ser296/297.

claim: The pThr306/pThr310 antiserum showed no significant detection of hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP in vehicle-treated cells.
source: Similar studies were performed with the putative pThr306/pThr310 antiserum on samples induced to express hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP. In this case there was no significant detection of the receptor construct in samples from vehicle-treated cells (Figure 2B)
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 2B shows minimal or no signal in vehicle-treated samples with pThr306/pThr310 antiserum.

claim: The pThr306/pThr310 antiserum showed strong identification of hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP after exposure to MOMBA.
source: however, after exposure to MOMBA there was also strong identification of diffuse polypeptide(s) centred at 70 kDa corresponding to hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP (Figure 2B).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 2B shows strong signal after MOMBA treatment with pThr306/pThr310 antiserum.

claim: The pThr306/pThr310 antiserum failed to detect hFFAR2-DREADD-PD2 (Thr306Ala/Thr310Ala variant) after MOMBA treatment.
source: Such staining was absent, however, when a variant hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP, in which in this case both Thr306 and Thr310 were altered to Ala (hFFAR2-DREADD-PD2), was induced (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 2B shows absence of signal for PD2 variant, confirming specificity of the antiserum for phosphorylated Thr306/310.

claim: MOMBA promoted interactions of hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP with arrestin-3 in a concentration-dependent manner with pEC50=4.62±0.13 M.
source: MOMBA promoted such interactions with the intact DREADD receptor construct in a concentration-dependent manner with pEC50=4.62±0.13 M (mean± SEM, n=3).
evidence: BRET-based arrestin-3 recruitment assay data shown in Figure 2C provides concentration-response measurements.

claim: The maximal effect of MOMBA on arrestin-3 recruitment was reduced for all phospho-deficient variants except hFFAR2-DREADD-PD2.
source: The maximal effect, but not measured potency, of MOMBA was reduced for all the PD variants except hFFAR2-DREADD-PD2 (Figure 2C), but in no case was the effect on maximal signal reduced by more than 50%.
evidence: BRET data in Figure 2C shows reduced maximal responses for PD1, PD3, and PD4 variants but not PD2.

claim: The hFFAR2-DREADD-PD1-4 variant (with all C-terminal phospho-acceptor sites mutated to alanine) was poorly able to recruit arrestin-3 in response to MOMBA (20.8±2.3% of wild-type receptor).
source: This variant was poorly able to recruit arrestin-3 (20.8±2.3% of wild-type receptor, mean ± SD, n=3) in response to addition of MOMBA (Figure 2C).
evidence: BRET data in Figure 2C shows dramatically reduced arrestin-3 recruitment for the PD1-4 variant.

claim: Pre-treatment with the GRK2/GRK3 selective inhibitor compound 101 greatly reduced MOMBA-induced interaction of hFFAR2-DREADD with arrestin-3.
source: It is likely that GRK2 and/or GRK3 played a key role in allowing MOMBA-induced interaction with arrestin-3 because this was greatly reduced when cells expressing the wild-type form of the receptor construct were pre-treated with the GRK2/GRK3 selective inhibitor compound 101 (Marsango et al., 2022; Figure 2D).
evidence: BRET data in Figure 2D shows reduced arrestin-3 recruitment after compound 101 treatment.

claim: Pre-treatment with compound 101 did not substantially reduce MOMBA-mediated identification of hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP by the pThr306/pThr310 antiserum.
source: Pre-treatment with compound 101 did not substantially reduce MOMBA-mediated identification by either the pThr306/pThr310 antiserum or the pSer296/pSer297 antiserum (Figure 2E).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 2E shows similar levels of phosphorylation detection with and without compound 101 treatment.

claim: Pre-treatment with compound 101 did not substantially reduce MOMBA-mediated identification of hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP by the pSer296/pSer297 antiserum.
source: Pre-treatment with compound 101 did not substantially reduce MOMBA-mediated identification by either the pThr306/pThr310 antiserum or the pSer296/pSer297 antiserum (Figure 2E).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 2E shows similar levels of phosphorylation detection with and without compound 101 treatment.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser296/Ser297 and Thr306/Thr310 are not controlled by GRK2/3.
source: This suggests that phosphorylation of these sites are not controlled by GRK2/3 and that these are not, at least in isolation, sufficient to define interactions of the receptor with arrestin-3.
evidence: Inference drawn from the observation that compound 101 (GRK2/3 inhibitor) does not reduce phosphorylation at these sites (Figure 2E) but does reduce arrestin-3 recruitment (Figure 2D).

claim: Sorbic acid promoted enhanced phosphorylation of Ser296/Ser297 in hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP.
source: The selective effect of the hFFAR2-DREADD agonist MOMBA in promoting enhanced phosphorylation of Ser296/Ser297 and in allowing phosphorylation of Thr306/Thr310 was further substantiated because both these effects of MOMBA were re-capitulated by the second hFFAR2-DREADD-specific agonist, sorbic acid (Bolognini et al., 2019; Hudson et al., 2012a; Figure 3A).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 3A shows similar effects of sorbic acid and MOMBA on receptor phosphorylation.

claim: Sorbic acid allowed phosphorylation of Thr306/Thr310 in hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP.
source: The selective effect of the hFFAR2-DREADD agonist MOMBA in promoting enhanced phosphorylation of Ser296/Ser297 and in allowing phosphorylation of Thr306/Thr310 was further substantiated because both these effects of MOMBA were re-capitulated by the second hFFAR2-DREADD-specific agonist, sorbic acid (Bolognini et al., 2019; Hudson et al., 2012a; Figure 3A).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 3A shows similar effects of sorbic acid and MOMBA on receptor phosphorylation.

claim: Propionic acid (C3) was unable to modulate the basal levels of phosphorylation detected by the pSer296/pSer297 antiserum in hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP.
source: By contrast, propionic acid (C3) which, as an SCFA, is an endogenous activator of wild-type hFFAR2 but does not activate hFFAR2-DREADD (Bolognini et al., 2019), was unable to modulate the basal levels of phosphorylation detected by the pSer296/pSer297 antiserum or to promote detection of the receptor by the pThr306/pThr310 antiserum (Figure 3A).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 3A shows no change in pSer296/pSer297 signal after C3 treatment of hFFAR2-DREADD.

claim: Propionic acid (C3) was unable to promote detection of hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP by the pThr306/pThr310 antiserum.
source: By contrast, propionic acid (C3) which, as an SCFA, is an endogenous activator of wild-type hFFAR2 but does not activate hFFAR2-DREADD (Bolognini et al., 2019), was unable to modulate the basal levels of phosphorylation detected by the pSer296/pSer297 antiserum or to promote detection of the receptor by the pThr306/pThr310 antiserum (Figure 3A).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 3A shows no pThr306/pThr310 signal after C3 treatment of hFFAR2-DREADD.

claim: Pre-addition of CATPB prevented the effects of MOMBA on receptor recognition by both the pSer296/pSer297 and the pThr306/pThr310 antisera.
source: Indeed, pre-addition of CATPB (10 mM) to cells induced to express hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP prevented the effects of MOMBA on receptor recognition by both the putative pSer296/pSer297 and the pThr306/pThr310 antisera (Figure 3B).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 3B shows absence of MOMBA-induced phosphorylation signals when CATPB is present.

claim: Pre-addition of CATPB lowered the extent of basal detection of hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP by the pSer296/pSer297 antiserum.
source: Additionally, pre-addition of CATPB lowered the extent of basal detection of the receptor by the pSer296/pSer297 antiserum (Figure 3B).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 3B shows reduced basal signal with CATPB treatment.

claim: At least part of the basal pSer296/pSer297 signal reflects agonist-independent, constitutive activity of hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP.
source: As CATPB possesses inverse agonist properties (Hudson et al., 2012b) this may indicate that at least part of the basal pSer296/pSer297 signal reflects agonist-independent, constitutive activity of hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP.
evidence: Inference based on the observation that the inverse agonist CATPB reduces basal phosphorylation (Figure 3B) and the known inverse agonist properties of CATPB.

claim: Treatment with lambda protein phosphatase (LPP) eliminated MOMBA-induced detection of hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP by both pSer296/pSer297 and pThr306/pThr310 antisera.
source: Now, MOMBA-induced detection of the receptor by both pSer296/pSer297 and pThr306/pThr310 antisera was eliminated (Figure 3B), as was most of the agonist-independent detection by pSer296/pSer297 (Figure 3B).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 3B shows loss of signal after LPP treatment, confirming that the antisera detect phosphorylated forms.

claim: The anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum was only able to identify hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP in immunocytochemistry after treatment with MOMBA.
source: However, also in this setting, the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum was only able to identify the receptor after treatment with MOMBA (Figure 3C)
evidence: Immunocytochemistry data in Figure 3C shows pThr306/pThr310 signal only in MOMBA-treated cells.

claim: Pre-addition of CATPB prevented the effect of MOMBA on detection of hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP by the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum in immunocytochemistry.
source: and, once again, pre-addition of CATPB prevented the effect of MOMBA (Figure 3C) without affecting direct identification and imaging of the receptor via the eYFP tag.
evidence: Immunocytochemistry data in Figure 3C shows absence of pThr306/pThr310 signal when CATPB is co-administered with MOMBA.

claim: Identification of hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP by the pSer296/pSer297 antiserum in immunocytochemistry was almost entirely dependent on exposure to MOMBA.
source: In this setting identification of hFFAR2 DREADD-eYFP by the pSer296/pSer297 antiserum was almost entirely dependent on exposure to MOMBA (Figure 3D)
evidence: Immunocytochemistry data in Figure 3D shows strong pSer296/pSer297 signal primarily in MOMBA-treated cells.

claim: Pre-treatment with CATPB prevented MOMBA-induced detection of hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP by the pSer296/pSer297 antiserum in immunocytochemistry.
source: and this was also prevented by pre-treatment with CATPB (Figure 3D).
evidence: Immunocytochemistry data in Figure 3D shows absence of MOMBA-induced pSer296/pSer297 signal when CATPB is present.

claim: FFAR2 is expressed in white adipose tissue.
source: FFAR2 is known to be expressed in white adipose tissue and we previously used these hFFAR2-DREADD-HA mice to define the role of this receptor as an anti-lipolytic regulator (Bolognini et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to previous work.

claim: hFFAR2-DREADD-HA was detected predominantly as an approximately 45 kDa species in white adipose tissue, with lower levels of a 40 kDa form.
source: Following SDS-PAGE of such immune precipitates from hFFAR2-DREADD-HA mice immunoblotting with an HA antibody resulted in detection of hFFAR2-DREADD-HA predominantly as an approximately 45 kDa species, with lower levels of a 40 kDa form (Figure 4A).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 4A shows the molecular weight distribution of the receptor in white adipose tissue.

claim: The pSer296/pSer297 antiserum detected hFFAR2-DREADD-HA in white adipose tissue without prior addition of a ligand.
source: Notably, immunoblotting of such samples with the anti-pSer296/pSer297 antiserum also detected the same polypeptides. However, unlike the hFFAR2 C-terminal tail antiserum, although the pSer296/pSer297 antiserum did identify hFFAR2-DREADD-HA without prior addition of a ligand, pre-addition of MOMBA increased immune detection of the receptor (Figure 4A).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 4A shows basal pSer296/pSer297 signal in vehicle-treated white adipose tissue.

claim: Pre-addition of MOMBA increased immune detection of hFFAR2-DREADD-HA by the pSer296/pSer297 antiserum in white adipose tissue.
source: pre-addition of MOMBA increased immune detection of the receptor (Figure 4A). This is consistent with the ligand promoting quantitatively greater levels of phosphorylation of these residues (Figure 4B).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 4A and quantification in Figure 4B show increased pSer296/pSer297 signal after MOMBA treatment.

claim: The anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum failed to detect immunoprecipitated hFFAR2-DREADD-HA from white adipose tissue in either the basal state or post-addition of MOMBA.
source: In contrast, the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum failed to detect immunoprecipitated hFFAR2-DREADD-HA from white adipose tissue in either the basal state or post-addition of MOMBA (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 4A and quantification in Figure 4B show no pThr306/pThr310 signal in white adipose tissue.

claim: Thr306 and Thr310 are not and do not become phosphorylated in white adipose tissue.
source: This indicates that these sites are not and do not become phosphorylated in this tissue.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the absence of pThr306/pThr310 signal in white adipose tissue (Figure 4A and B).

claim: Clear identification of pSer296/pSer297 hFFAR2-DREADD-HA was detected in fixed adipose tissue from hFFAR2-DREADD-HA-expressing mice that had been pre-exposed to MOMBA.
source: Immunohistochemical studies performed on fixed adipose tissue from hFFAR2-DREADD-HA-expressing mice that had been pre-exposed to MOMBA were consistent with the immunoblotting studies. Clear identification of pSer296/pSer297 hFFAR2-DREADD-HA was detected and the specificity of this was confirmed by the absence of staining in equivalent samples from CRE-MINUS mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data in Figure 4C shows pSer296/pSer297 staining in MOMBA-treated adipose tissue from hFFAR2-DREADD-HA mice but not CRE-MINUS mice.

claim: No specific staining was observed for the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum in adipose tissue from hFFAR2-DREADD-HA-expressing mice.
source: Once more, no specific staining was observed for the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum (Figure 4C).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data in Figure 4C shows absence of pThr306/pThr310 staining in adipose tissue.

claim: Clear detection of pSer296/pSer297 immunostaining was observed in adipose tissue from hFFAR2-DREADD-HA mice without exposure to MOMBA.
source: Clear detection of pSer296/pSer297 immunostaining was observed in adipose tissue from hFFAR2-DREADD-HA mice without exposure to MOMBA but once more the intensity of staining was markedly increased after MOMBA treatment (Figure 4D).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data in Figure 4D shows basal pSer296/pSer297 staining in vehicle-treated adipose tissue.

claim: The intensity of pSer296/pSer297 staining in adipose tissue was markedly increased after MOMBA treatment.
source: Clear detection of pSer296/pSer297 immunostaining was observed in adipose tissue from hFFAR2-DREADD-HA mice without exposure to MOMBA but once more the intensity of staining was markedly increased after MOMBA treatment (Figure 4D).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data in Figure 4D shows increased pSer296/pSer297 staining intensity after MOMBA treatment.

claim: pSer296/pSer297 hFFAR2-DREADD-HA is present directly on adipocytes.
source: and clear co-localisation of anti- pSer296/pSer297 immunostaining with that for perilipin-1 (Figure 4F) confirmed the presence of pSer296/pSer297 hFFAR2-DREADD-HA directly on adipocytes.
evidence: Co-localization data in Figure 4F shows overlap of pSer296/pSer297 signal with perilipin-1, an adipocyte marker.

claim: Anti-HA staining showed extensive and high-level expression of hFFAR2-DREADD-HA in cells within Peyer's patches.
source: Anti-HA staining showed extensive and high-level expression of hFFAR2-DREADD-HA in cells within these structures (Figure 5A).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5A shows widespread HA staining in Peyer's patches.

claim: Many of the hFFAR2-DREADD-HA-positive cells in Peyer's patches correspond to dendritic cells, monocytes, and/or macrophages.
source: Co-staining for CD11c indicated many of the hFFAR2-DREADD-HA-positive cells correspond to dendritic cells, monocytes, and/or macrophages (Figure 5B).
evidence: Co-localization data in Figure 5B shows overlap of HA signal with CD11c, a marker for these immune cell types.

claim: hFFAR2-DREADD-HA is well expressed by type-III innate lymphoid cells in Peyer's patches.
source: Co-staining to detect the presence of the nuclear transcription factor RoRγt also indicated, as shown previously at the mRNA level for mouse FFAR2 (Chun et al., 2019), that hFFAR2-DREADD-HA is well expressed by type-III innate lymphoid cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: Co-localization data in Figure 5C shows overlap of HA signal with RoRγt, a marker for type-III innate lymphoid cells, and is supported by previous mRNA expression data.

claim: hFFAR2-DREADD-HA in Peyer's patches showed a more diffuse pattern of immunostaining than observed from white adipose tissue, potentially reflecting a more complex pattern of post-translational modifications.
source: Anti-HA immunoblotting of such material indicated a more diffuse pattern of immunostaining than observed from white adipose tissue (Figure 5D). This may reflect a more complex pattern of post-translational modifications, including differing extents of N-glycosylation (see later) than observed in white adipose tissue (compare Figure 5D with Figure 4A).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 5D shows broader molecular weight distribution compared to Figure 4A, suggesting different post-translational modifications.

claim: In Peyer's patches, hFFAR2-DREADD-HA became phosphorylated on Thr306/Thr310 in a MOMBA-dependent manner, with no detection of phosphorylation of these residues without agonist treatment.
source: Parallel immunoblots of such samples with the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum now indicated that, in contrast to adipocytes, hFFAR2-DREADD-HA became phosphorylated on these residues in a MOMBA-dependent manner, with no detection of phosphorylation of these residues without agonist treatment (Figure 5D).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 5D shows pThr306/pThr310 signal only after MOMBA treatment in Peyer's patches.

claim: The effect of MOMBA on pThr306/pThr310 phosphorylation in Peyer's patches was clearly mediated by the hFFAR2-DREADD-HA receptor because anti-pThr306/pThr310 recognition was entirely lacking when MOMBA was added after the addition of CATPB.
source: Moreover, this effect of MOMBA was clearly mediated by the hFFAR2-DREADD-HA receptor because anti-pThr306/pThr310 recognition was entirely lacking when MOMBA was added after the addition of the hFFAR2 antagonist/inverse agonist CATPB (Figure 5D and E) that blocks this receptor with high affinity (Hudson et al., 2012b; Hudson et al., 2013).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 5D and quantification in Figure 5E show absence of pThr306/pThr310 signal when CATPB is co-administered with MOMBA.

claim: Basal detection of hFFAR2-DREADD-HA by the anti-pSer296/pSer297 antiserum in Peyer's patches was low and was increased markedly by pre-treatment with MOMBA.
source: Similar outcomes were obtained in this tissue with the anti-pSer296/pSer297 antiserum. Basal detection of the immune-captured receptor was low and this was increased markedly by pre-treatment with MOMBA (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 5D and quantification in Figure 5E show low basal and increased MOMBA-induced pSer296/pSer297 signal in Peyer's patches.

claim: The effect of MOMBA on pSer296/pSer297 phosphorylation in Peyer's patches was not observed when cells were exposed to CATPB in addition to MOMBA.
source: As for the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum the effect of MOMBA on recognition of the receptor was not observed when cells were exposed to CATPB in addition to MOMBA (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 5D and quantification in Figure 5E show absence of MOMBA-induced pSer296/pSer297 signal when CATPB is present.

claim: Immunostaining of fixed Peyer's patch tissue with the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum confirmed the marked agonist dependence of recognition of hFFAR2-DREADD-HA in such cells.
source: Immunostaining of fixed Peyer's patch tissue with the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum confirmed the marked agonist dependence of recognition of hFFAR2-DREADD-HA in such cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5F shows pThr306/pThr310 staining primarily in MOMBA-treated Peyer's patches.

claim: Immunostaining with the pSer296/pSer297 antiserum in Peyer's patches indicated a degree of agonist-independent phosphorylation of these sites.
source: In this tissue, immunostaining with the pSer296/pSer297 antiserum indicated a degree of agonist-independent phosphorylation of these sites as this was not observed in tissue from CRE-MINUS mice, and a further increase in staining following pre-treatment with MOMBA was evident (Figure 5F).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data in Figure 5F shows basal pSer296/pSer297 staining in vehicle-treated Peyer's patches from hFFAR2-DREADD-HA mice but not CRE-MINUS mice, with increased staining after MOMBA.

claim: Addition of MOMBA to colonic epithelia produced a limited number of widely dispersed cells identified by the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum, with minimal staining of vehicle-treated controls.
source: To extend this we added vehicle or MOMBA to preparations of colonic epithelia from these mice. Subsequent immunostaining with the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum identified a limited number of widely dispersed cells in MOMBA-treated tissue but minimal staining of the vehicle-treated controls (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data in Figure 6A and B shows sparse pThr306/pThr310-positive cells in MOMBA-treated colonic tissue.

claim: Similar experiments with the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum on colonic tissue from CRE-MINUS mice failed to identify equivalent cells.
source: As an additional specificity control similar experiments were performed with the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum on tissue from the CRE-MINUS mice. These failed to identify equivalent cells (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data in Figure 6A and B shows absence of pThr306/pThr310 staining in CRE-MINUS colonic tissue.

claim: Specific agonist-mediated immuno-recognition of hFFAR2-DREADD-HA with both the anti-pThr306/pThr310 and anti-pSer296/pSer297 antisera was detected in colonic tissue, but was challenging to detect.
source: Despite the limited cell expression pattern of anti-HA detected previously in colonic tissue (Bolognini et al., 2019), we were again able to specifically capture hFFAR2-DREADD-HA via HA pull-down (Figure 6C). Here, although challenging to detect, we were able to record specific agonist-mediated immuno-recognition of polypeptides of the appropriate molecular mass with both the anti-pThr306/pThr310 and anti-pSer296/pSer297 antisera that were again absent following HA pull-downs conducted in tissue from CRE-MINUS mice (Figure 6C).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 6C shows weak but specific signals for both phospho-antisera in MOMBA-treated colonic tissue from hFFAR2-DREADD-HA mice but not CRE-MINUS mice.

claim: Compared to white adipose tissue or Peyer's patch immune cells, detection of pThr306/pThr310 or pSer296/pSer297 in colonic epithelial cells was modest and potentially indicated only limited phosphorylation of these sites, even after exposure to MOMBA.
source: However, compared to the intensity of immunodetection of either anti-pThr306/pThr310 or anti-pSer296/pSer297 in white adipose tissue or Peyer's patch immune cells compared to the extent of anti-HA pull-down, such detection was modest and potentially indicted only limited phosphorylation of these sites in such colonic epithelial cells, even after exposure to MOMBA (Figure 6C).
evidence: Comparison of immunoblot signal intensities across Figure 4A, Figure 5D, and Figure 6C shows weaker phosphorylation signals in colonic tissue relative to receptor expression levels.

claim: Addition of C3 to Peyer's patches from hFFAR2-HA-expressing mice produced a marked increase in detection of hFFAR2-HA by the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum compared to vehicle-treated samples.
source: In immunocytochemical studies using Peyer's patches isolated from the hFFAR2-HA-expressing mice addition of C3 (10 mM, 20 min) produced a marked increase in detection of hFFAR2-HA by the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum compared to vehicle-treated samples (Figure 8A).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data in Figure 8A shows increased pThr306/pThr310 staining after C3 treatment in Peyer's patches from hFFAR2-HA mice.

claim: The effect of C3 on pThr306/pThr310 detection was lacking in Peyer's patches from CRE-MINUS mice.
source: By contrast, such an effect of C3 was lacking in equivalent tissue isolated from equivalent CRE-MINUS comparator mice (Figure 8A).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data in Figure 8A shows no change in pThr306/pThr310 staining after C3 treatment in CRE-MINUS Peyer's patches.

claim: Basal identification of anti-pSer296/pSer297 staining in Peyer's patches from hFFAR2-HA mice was significant and little altered by treatment with C3.
source: Basal identification of anti-pSer296/pSer297 staining was significant (Figure 8B) and little altered by treatment with C3 (Figure 8B).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data in Figure 8B shows substantial basal pSer296/pSer297 staining with minimal change after C3 treatment.

claim: Basal phosphorylation of Ser296/Ser297 in Peyer's patches from hFFAR2-HA mice appeared to be specific, as it was lacking in tissue from CRE-MINUS mice.
source: Such basal phosphorylation of Ser296/Ser297 did appear to be specific however, as this was lacking in tissue from the CRE-MINUS mice (Figure 8B).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data in Figure 8B shows pSer296/pSer297 staining in hFFAR2-HA mice but not CRE-MINUS mice.

claim: Immunoblotting with the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum showed clear phosphorylation of pThr306/pThr310 in Peyer's patches from hFFAR2-HA mice in response to C3 that increased from essentially undetectable levels in vehicle-treated cells.
source: Immunoblotting such samples with the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum showed clear phosphorylation of pThr306/pThr310 in response to C3 (Figure 8C) that increased from essentially undetectable levels in samples of vehicle-treated cells (Figure 8D).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 8C and quantification in Figure 8D show C3-induced pThr306/pThr310 signal in Peyer's patches from hFFAR2-HA mice.

claim: The effect of C3 on pThr306/pThr310 phosphorylation in Peyer's patches from hFFAR2-HA mice was clearly produced directly at the hFFAR2-HA receptor because pre-treatment with CATPB entirely blocked the effect of C3.
source: Like cells from hFFAR2-DREADD-HA-expressing Peyer's patches the effect of C3 was clearly produced directly at the hFFAR2-HA receptor because pre-treatment with CATPB entirely blocked the effect of C3 (Figure 8C and D).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 8C and quantification in Figure 8D show absence of C3-induced pThr306/pThr310 signal when CATPB is present.

claim: The anti-pSer296/pSer297 antiserum showed enhanced detection of hFFAR2-HA in Peyer's patches in response to treatment with C3 that was prevented by pre-treatment with CATPB.
source: The anti-pSer296/pSer297 antiserum also showed enhanced detection of hFFAR2-HA in response to treatment with C3 in this setting that was also prevented by pre-treatment with CATPB (Figure 8C and D)
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 8C and quantification in Figure 8D show C3-induced increase in pSer296/pSer297 signal that is blocked by CATPB.

claim: The enhancement of pSer296/pSer297 detection by C3 in Peyer's patches appeared to be less pronounced than the enhancement of pThr306/pThr310 detection.
source: but this appeared to be less pronounced than in the studies employing anti-pThr306/pThr310 hFFAR2.
evidence: Comparison of signal changes in Figure 8C and D suggests differential magnitude of C3-induced phosphorylation at the two sites.

claim: Similar levels of hFFAR2-DREADD-HA and hFFAR2-HA were observed in both white adipose tissue and colonic epithelial preparations from homozygous animals of each transgenic line.
source: To assess the relative expression of hFFAR2-HA in this line compared to hFFAR2-DREADD-HA in equivalent tissues of the hFFAR2-DREADD-HA knock-in mice, we isolated both white adipocytes and colonic epithelia from homozygous animals of each line and immunoprecipitated the corresponding receptors using anti-HA. Immunoblotting of such HA immunoprecipitates showed similar levels of the corresponding receptor in each and that the molecular mass of hFFAR2-HA was equivalent to hFFAR2-DREADD-HA (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 shows comparable expression levels and molecular weights of the two receptor constructs.

claim: Immunoblots using anti-GFP confirmed similar levels of hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP in vehicle and C3-treated samples.
source: Parallel immunoblotting with anti-GFP confirmed the presence of similar levels of hFFAR2-eYFP both with and without treatment with C3 (Figure 7A)
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 7A shows equivalent anti-GFP signal across treatment conditions.

claim: Expression of hFFAR2-eYFP was lacking if cells harbouring hFFAR2-eYFP had not been induced with doxycycline.
source: and confirmed in addition that expression of the receptor construct was lacking if cells harbouring hFFAR2-eYFP had not been induced with doxycycline (Figure 7A).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 7A shows no signal in -dox lanes.

claim: C3-induced recognition of hFFAR2-eYFP by the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum was lacking in the co-presence of the hFFAR2 antagonist CATPB.
source: As with the effect of MOMBA on the hFFAR2-DREADD-eYFP construct, in studies using the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum, C3-induced recognition of the hFFAR2-eYFP receptor was lacking in the co-presence of the hFFAR2 antagonist CATPB (Figure 7B).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 7B shows absence of C3-induced pThr306/pThr310 signal when CATPB is present.

claim: Treatment of C3-exposed samples with lambda protein phosphatase before SDS-PAGE prevented subsequent hFFAR2-eYFP identification by the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum.
source: In addition, treatment of C3-exposed samples to LPP before SDS-PAGE also prevented subsequent hFFAR2-eYFP identification by the anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum (Figure 7B), confirming this to reflect phosphorylation of the target.
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 7B shows loss of pThr306/pThr310 signal after LPP treatment, confirming phosphorylation-dependent detection.

claim: The anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum was only able to identify hFFAR2-eYFP in immunocytochemistry after exposure to C3.
source: The anti-pThr306/pThr310 antiserum was only able to identify hFFAR2-eYFP after exposure to C3 in this context (Figure 7C)
evidence: Immunocytochemistry data in Figure 7C shows pThr306/pThr310 signal only in C3-treated cells.

claim: The anti-pSer296/pSer297 antiserum identified wild-type hFFAR2-eYFP in both vehicle and C3-treated cells in immunocytochemistry.
source: whereas for this construct the anti-pSer296/pSer297 antiserum identified the receptor in both vehicle and C3-treated cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: Immunocytochemistry data in Figure 7D shows pSer296/pSer297 signal in both vehicle and C3-treated cells.

claim: Co-translational N-glycosylation, and potentially other post-translational modifications, of the hFFAR2-DREADD-HA receptor was markedly different in various tissues.
source: A further interesting feature, although not inherently linked to bar-coding, is that co-translational N-glycosylation, and potentially other post-translational modifications, of the hFFAR2-DREADD-HA receptor (and probably of hFFAR2-HA) was markedly different in these various tissues.
evidence: Observation based on differences in molecular weight patterns across tissues shown in immunoblots (Figures 4A, 5D, 6C).

claim: The predominant form of hFFAR2-DREADD-HA in colonic epithelium migrated as a substantially larger species than that isolated from white adipocytes.
source: As we were able to use the HA tag to immunoprecipitate the receptor from different tissues, SDS-PAGE and immunoblotting studies showed that the predominant form of the receptor in colonic epithelium migrated as a substantially larger species than that isolated from white adipocytes, and this was also the case when the receptor was immune-enriched from Peyer's patches and associated mesenteric lymph nodes (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Immunoblot data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2 shows different molecular weight distributions of the receptor across tissues.

claim: Differences in molecular weight of hFFAR2-DREADD-HA across tissues reflect, at least in part, differential extents of N-glycosylation.
source: De-glycosylation studies using an enzyme able to cleave N-linked carbohydrate confirmed these differences to reflect, at least in part, differential extents of N-glycosylation (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: De-glycosylation experiment data in Figure 8—figure supplement 2 shows altered molecular weight after N-glycosidase F treatment.

claim: The same agonist-receptor pairing generates distinct phosphorylation patterns in distinct patho-physiologically relevant tissues.
source: Despite this, the current studies show clear evidence of how the same ligand-GPCR pairing generates distinct phosphorylation patterns and hence different 'bar-codes' in distinct patho-physiologically relevant tissues.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from the differential phosphorylation patterns observed across white adipose tissue, Peyer's patches, and colonic epithelium (Figures 4, 5, 6).

claim: FFAR2 is expressed widely, including in white adipocytes and various immune and enteroendocrine cells.
source: Free fatty acid receptor 2 (FFAR2) is activated by short-chain fatty acids and expressed widely, including in white adipocytes and various immune and enteroendocrine cells.
evidence: Statement in the abstract summarizing known expression pattern.

claim: In white adipose tissue, phosphorylation of residues Ser296/Ser297 was enhanced upon agonist activation.
source: In white adipose tissue, phosphorylation of residues Ser296/Ser297 was enhanced upon agonist activation whilst Thr306/Thr310 did not become phosphorylated.
evidence: Summary statement in abstract supported by data in Figures 4A, 4B, 4D.

claim: In white adipose tissue, Thr306/Thr310 did not become phosphorylated.
source: In white adipose tissue, phosphorylation of residues Ser296/Ser297 was enhanced upon agonist activation whilst Thr306/Thr310 did not become phosphorylated.
evidence: Summary statement in abstract supported by data in Figures 4A, 4B, 4C.

claim: In immune cells from Peyer's patches, Thr306/Thr310 become phosphorylated in a strictly agonist-dependent fashion.
source: By contrast, in immune cells from Peyer's patches Thr306/Thr310 become phosphorylated in a strictly agonist-dependent fashion
evidence: Summary statement in abstract supported by data in Figures 5D, 5E, 5F.

claim: In enteroendocrine cells of the colon, both Ser296/Ser297 and Thr306/Thr310 were poorly phosphorylated.
source: whilst in enteroendocrine cells of the colon both Ser296/Ser297 and Thr306/Thr310 were poorly phosphorylated.
evidence: Summary statement in abstract supported by data in Figure 6C.

claim: The concept of phosphorylation bar-coding has centred to date on the potential for different agonists to promote distinct receptor phosphorylation patterns.
source: The concept of phosphorylation bar-coding has centred to date on the potential for different agonists to promote distinct receptor phosphorylation patterns.
evidence: Statement summarizing the existing understanding of phosphorylation bar-coding in the field.

claim: Tissue-specific phosphorylation bar-coding may underpin why a single G protein-coupled receptor can generate different functional outcomes in a tissue-specific manner.
source: This may underpin why a single G protein-coupled receptor can generate different functional outcomes in a tissue-specific manner.
evidence: Speculative conclusion drawn from the observed tissue-specific phosphorylation patterns.

claim: GPCRs routinely are constitutively phosphorylated or become phosphorylated on serine and threonine residues following exposure to activating agonist ligands.
source: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) routinely are constitutively phosphorylated or become phosphorylated on serine and threonine residues, located either within the third intracellular loop or the C-terminal tail, following exposure to activating agonist ligands (Zhang et al., 2022).
evidence: General statement about GPCR phosphorylation supported by citation.

claim: GPCR phosphorylation is generally accompanied by new or enhanced interactions with arrestin adapter proteins.
source: This is generally accompanied by new or enhanced interactions with arrestin adapter proteins.
evidence: General statement about GPCR signaling based on established knowledge.

claim: Arrestin binding to GPCRs results in receptor desensitisation because the positioning of the arrestin precludes simultaneous interactions of the GPCR with a heterotrimeric G protein.
source: Canonically this results in receptor desensitisation because the positioning of the arrestin precludes simultaneous interactions of the GPCR with a heterotrimeric guanine nucleotide binding (G) protein and hence 'arrests' further G protein activation (Sun and Kim, 2021).
evidence: Canonical mechanism of GPCR desensitisation supported by citation.

claim: Receptors exist in multiply phosphorylated states where numerous kinases are involved.
source: The earliest studies on GPCR phosphorylation determined that receptors exist in multiply phosphorylated states where numerous kinases, that include members of the G protein receptor kinase (GRK) family, second messenger-regulated kinases, and even those of the casein kinase family are involved (Pitcher et al., 1998; Budd et al., 2000; Torrecilla et al., 2007).
evidence: Historical observation about GPCR phosphorylation supported by multiple citations.

claim: The pattern of receptor phosphorylation was distinct among cell types and tissues.
source: Using mass spectrometry approaches and phospho-site-specific antibodies it emerged that the pattern of receptor phosphorylation was distinct among cell types and tissues (Tran et al., 2004; Nobles et al., 2011; Kaya et al., 2020).
evidence: Observation from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: The tissue-specific signalling output of GPCRs might be determined, at least in part, by the pattern of receptor phosphorylation.
source: This led to the notion that the tissue-specific signalling output of GPCRs might be determined, at least in part, by the pattern of receptor phosphorylation – a hypothesis coined the phosphorylation barcode (Nobles et al., 2011; Tobin et al., 2008).
evidence: Hypothesis from the field supported by citations.

claim: The conformation adopted by an arrestin on interaction with the phosphorylated form of a GPCR might be affected by the pattern of receptor phosphorylation.
source: This notion has recently been taken a step further with appreciation that the conformation adopted by an arrestin on interaction with the phosphorylated form of a GPCR might be affected by the pattern of receptor phosphorylation and in turn this may affect the signalling outputs mediated by arrestins (Latorraca et al., 2020).
evidence: Recent development in the field supported by citation.

claim: Short chain fatty acids are generated in prodigious quantities by fermentation of dietary fibre by the gut microbiota.
source: A number of GPCRs are able to bind and respond to short chain fatty acids (SCFAs) that are generated in prodigious quantities by fermentation of dietary fibre by the gut microbiota (Xie et al., 2023; Tan et al., 2023).
evidence: Established biological fact supported by citations.

claim: FFAR2 is the most studied and best characterised GPCR that responds to short chain fatty acids.
source: The most studied and best characterised of these is FFAR2 (also designated GPR43) (Bolognini et al., 2016b; Stoddart et al., 2008; Ikeda et al., 2022).
evidence: Statement about the state of the field supported by citations.

claim: FFAR2 is expressed by a range of immune cells, adipocytes, enteroendocrine, and pancreatic cells.
source: This receptor is expressed widely, including by a range of immune cells, adipocytes, enteroendocrine, and pancreatic cells (Bolognini et al., 2016b; Stoddart et al., 2008; Ikeda et al., 2022).
evidence: Known expression pattern supported by citations.

claim: FFAR2 is able to couple to a range of different heterotrimeric G proteins from each of the Gi, Gq, and G12/G13 families when expressed in simple heterologous cell lines.
source: In addition to being widely expressed FFAR2 is, at least when expressed in simple heterologous cell lines, able to couple to a range of different heterotrimeric G proteins from each of the Gi, Gq, and G12/G13 families (Brown et al., 2003; Bolognini et al., 2019).
evidence: Known signaling properties supported by citations.

claim: In white adipocytes, stimulation of FFAR2 is anti-lipolytic, an effect mediated via pertussis toxin-sensitive Gi proteins and reduction in cellular cAMP levels.
source: For example, in white adipocytes stimulation of FFAR2 is clearly anti-lipolytic, an effect mediated via pertussis toxin-sensitive Gi proteins and reduction in cellular cAMP levels (Bolognini et al., 2016a)
evidence: Known functional effect in specific cell type supported by citation.

claim: In GLP-1-positive enteroendocrine cells, activation of FFAR2 promotes release of GLP-1 in a Ca2+ and Gq-mediated manner.
source: whilst in GLP-1-positive enteroendocrine cells activation of FFAR2 promotes release of this incretin hormone in a Ca2+ and Gq-mediated manner (Bolognini et al., 2016a).
evidence: Known functional effect in specific cell type supported by citation.

claim: The pharmacology of the various GPCRs that respond to SCFAs is very limited.
source: A challenge in studying the molecular basis of effects of SCFAs in native cells and tissues is that the pharmacology of the various GPCRs that respond to these ligands is very limited (Milligan et al., 2017a; Milligan et al., 2017b)
evidence: Known limitation in the field supported by citations.

claim: There is a particular dearth of antagonist ligands for anything other than the human ortholog of FFAR2.
source: and there is a particular dearth of antagonist ligands for anything other than the human ortholog of FFAR2 (Milligan et al., 2017a; Milligan et al., 2017b).
evidence: Known limitation in the field supported by citations.

claim: Designer receptor exclusively activated by designer drug (DREADD) forms of GPCRs contain mutations that eliminate binding and responsiveness to endogenously generated orthosteric agonists whilst allowing binding and activation by defined, non-endogenously produced ligands.
source: Designer receptor exclusively activated by designer drug (DREADD) forms of GPCRs contain mutations that eliminate binding and responsiveness to endogenously generated orthosteric agonists whilst, in parallel, allowing binding and activation by defined, but non-endogenously produced, ligands that do not activate the wild-type form of the receptor (Wang et al., 2021; Bradley et al., 2018; Shchepinova et al., 2020).
evidence: Definition and properties of DREADDs supported by citations.

claim: The hFFAR2-DREADD variant differs from wild-type receptor only in two amino acids of the orthosteric ligand binding pocket (Cys141Gly, His242Gln).
source: Moreover, as the DREADD variant differs from wild-type receptor only in two amino acids of the orthosteric ligand binding pocket, and the intracellular sections of the two forms are identical (Bolognini et al., 2019)
evidence: Structural information about the DREADD variant shown in Figure 2A and supported by citation.

claim: The intracellular sections of hFFAR2-DREADD and wild-type hFFAR2 are identical.
source: Moreover, as the DREADD variant differs from wild-type receptor only in two amino acids of the orthosteric ligand binding pocket, and the intracellular sections of the two forms are identical (Bolognini et al., 2019)
evidence: Structural information supported by citation.
